```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(
  collapse = FALSE,
  comment = "",
  class.output = "spax-output",
  fig.width = 7,
  fig.height = 4.5,
  dpi = 100,
  # cairo writes smaller PNG files than the default macOS device
  dev.args = if (capabilities("cairo")) list(type = "cairo") else list()
)
```

spax ships open data on general practice (GP) care in NHS Cornwall and the
Isles of Scilly, in south-west England, and the guides run on it. This page answers one
question: what is in the example data? It introduces each object once: what
it holds, how the objects fit together and what they cannot tell you. By the
end you can load each one and build the inputs that the guides start from.
Nothing needs downloading. The `spax()` interface and the allocation model are
experimental and may change in later versions.

The page uses spax with terra for the grids, sf for the points and polygons,
and dplyr and ggplot2 for tables and maps.

```{r packages, message = FALSE, warning = FALSE}
library(spax)
library(terra)
library(sf)
library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)
```

Four objects load with spax, and two grids are read from files:

| Object | What it holds | How to load it |
|:--|:--|:--|
| `cornwall_gp` | `r nrow(cornwall_gp)` GP practices: location, GP workforce and list size | Loaded with spax |
| `cornwall_lsoa` | `r nrow(cornwall_lsoa)` small areas: boundaries, population and registered residents | Loaded with spax |
| `cornwall_flows` | Registered residents by small area and practice | Loaded with spax |
| `cornwall_travel` | Travel minutes from each small area to each practice | Loaded with spax |
| `cornwall_pop.tif` | Population grid, about 1 km cells | `read_spax_example()` |
| `cornwall_gp_travel.tif` | Travel minutes from each grid cell to each practice | `read_spax_example()` |

Each object has a help page with every column, for example `?cornwall_gp`.

## Practices

`cornwall_gp` is an `sf` point layer in British National Grid coordinates
(EPSG:27700), one row per practice. `practice` is the NHS practice code, which
links the practices to the registrations and to the travel times. The code
drops the geometry and shows the first practices.

```{r practices}
gp <- st_drop_geometry(cornwall_gp)
gp |>
  select(practice, name, gp_fte_extg, gp_fte, list_size) |>
  head()
```

The guides use `gp_fte_extg` as supply, what each practice offers: full-time
equivalent GPs (37.5 hours a week) excluding GPs in training, from the June
2026 workforce data. GPs in training are left out because they cluster in a
few training practices. `gp_fte` includes them. `list_size` counts all patients
registered at the practice. Each
practice sits at its main site, so branch surgeries do not appear.

## Small areas

`cornwall_lsoa` holds the `r nrow(cornwall_lsoa)` Lower layer Super Output
Areas (LSOA 2021), small areas of
`r format(min(cornwall_lsoa$pop), big.mark = ",")` to
`r format(max(cornwall_lsoa$pop), big.mark = ",")` residents. Each has an ONS
mid-2024 population estimate (`pop`, also by age band) and the number of its
residents registered at any GP practice in England (`registered`). That number
splits into residents registered at a practice in Cornwall and the Isles of
Scilly (`registered_in`) and those registered elsewhere (`registered_out`).
The code adds up these columns and counts the areas in each broad rural-urban
class.

```{r small-areas}
areas <- st_drop_geometry(cornwall_lsoa)

c(
  population = sum(areas$pop),
  registered = sum(areas$registered),
  registered_in = sum(areas$registered_in),
  registered_out = sum(areas$registered_out)
)

# Rural-urban classification (2021), in three broad groups
table(sub(":.*", "", areas$ruc21))
```

`registered_in` and `registered_out` add up to `registered`. Registered
residents outnumber the population estimate by about
`r round(100 * (sum(areas$registered) / sum(areas$pop) - 1))`%, which reflects
list inflation (patients who stay on a list after moving away) and the
different reference dates. The map shows the small areas by broad rural-urban
class, with the practices on top.

```{r areas-map, fig.alt = sprintf("Map of the %d small areas of Cornwall and the Isles of Scilly colored by broad rural-urban class (urban, larger rural, smaller rural), with the %d GP practices as black points.", nrow(areas), nrow(gp))}
# Small areas with a broad rural-urban class
classed <- cornwall_lsoa |>
  mutate(class = sub(":.*", "", ruc21))

ggplot() +
  geom_sf(
    data = classed,
    aes(fill = class),
    color = "white",
    linewidth = 0.1
  ) +
  geom_sf(data = st_union(cornwall_lsoa), fill = NA, color = "grey20", linewidth = 0.3) +
  geom_sf(data = cornwall_gp, size = 1) +
  scale_fill_manual(
    name = "Rural-urban class",
    values = c(
      Urban = "#5b7fa6",
      `Larger rural` = "#a9c48f",
      `Smaller rural` = "#e3dca8"
    )
  ) +
  labs(title = "Small areas (LSOA 2021) and GP practices") +
  theme_void()
```

`r sum(grepl("^Urban", areas$ruc21))` of the `r nrow(areas)` areas are urban,
but they cover little land: the towns show as tight blue clusters, and most of
the county's land lies in smaller rural areas. The Isles of Scilly are the
small group of islands off the western tip.

## Registrations

`cornwall_flows` counts the residents of each small area registered at each of
the `r nrow(cornwall_gp)` practices, one row per pair with at least one
registration. The code shows the first rows, checks that each area's rows add
up to its `registered_in`, and counts the pairs.

```{r flows}
head(cornwall_flows)

# Each area's registrations add up to its registered_in
by_area <- tapply(cornwall_flows$patients, cornwall_flows$lsoa, sum)
all(by_area[areas$lsoa] == areas$registered_in)

c(
  pairs = nrow(cornwall_flows),
  registered_residents = sum(cornwall_flows$patients)
)
```

Every area's rows add up to its `registered_in`, so the flows hold all
`r format(sum(cornwall_flows$patients), big.mark = ",")` residents registered
inside Cornwall and the Isles of Scilly, spread over
`r format(nrow(cornwall_flows), big.mark = ",")` area-practice pairs.

A registration is a **stock**: who is registered with which practice on one
date (July 2026), not a count of visits. Residents counted in
`registered_out` are registered with a practice outside Cornwall and the Isles
of Scilly, for example in Devon, so they are in `cornwall_lsoa` but not in
these flows. The guides on the allocation model, a model of where each area's
residents register, fit it to these counts. The guides on floating catchment
area (FCA) indices, which measure supply per resident, do not use them.

## Travel times

`cornwall_travel` is a matrix of motorized travel minutes from each small
area's population-weighted centroid (rows, `cornwall_lsoa$lsoa`) to each
practice's main site (columns, `cornwall_gp$practice`). The code prints a
corner of the matrix and summarizes the minutes from each area to its nearest
practice.

```{r travel}
cornwall_travel[1:3, 1:4]

# Minutes from each small area to its nearest practice
nearest <- apply(cornwall_travel, 1, min, na.rm = TRUE)
summary(nearest)
```

The times are least-cost paths over a 2019 global map of the time needed to
cross each cell of about 1 km (a friction surface). They are rounded to whole
minutes, with a floor of one minute, so no time is 0.
`r sum(nearest == 1)` of the `r length(nearest)` small areas have a practice
at 1 minute. Traffic is not modeled. In towns several practices can share one
cell, so they have the same travel time from every area. The map shows the
time to the nearest practice.

```{r nearest-map, fig.alt = sprintf("Map of the small areas of Cornwall and the Isles of Scilly colored by travel minutes to the nearest GP practice, from %d to %d minutes; most areas are within a few minutes of a practice, and the longest times are at the western tip, inland in the north-east and in one area on the north coast near Padstow.", min(nearest), max(nearest))}
# Join each area's nearest-practice time to its polygon
nearest_map <- cornwall_lsoa |>
  mutate(minutes = nearest[lsoa])

ggplot(nearest_map) +
  geom_sf(aes(fill = minutes), color = "white", linewidth = 0.05) +
  geom_sf(data = st_union(cornwall_lsoa), fill = NA, color = "grey20", linewidth = 0.3) +
  scale_fill_viridis_c(name = "Minutes", option = "magma", direction = -1) +
  labs(title = "Travel time to the nearest GP practice") +
  theme_void()
```

Most small areas are within a few minutes of a practice. The map gives most of
its area to the large rural areas, so the many small town areas, mostly at 1
minute, are hard to see. The longest trips, up to `r max(nearest)` minutes,
are at the western tip, inland in the north-east and in one area on the north
coast near Padstow.

## The grids

Two GeoTIFF files cover the same 30 arc-second grid (about 1 km, in longitude
and latitude). `cornwall_pop.tif` holds WorldPop 2020 estimated residents per
cell: a **count**, not a density. `cornwall_gp_travel.tif` holds one layer of
travel minutes per practice, named by practice code. `read_spax_example()`
reads both, and the code counts their cells, layers and residents.

```{r grids}
pop <- read_spax_example("cornwall_pop.tif")
travel_grid <- read_spax_example("cornwall_gp_travel.tif")

c(
  cells = ncell(pop),
  populated_cells = sum(!is.na(values(pop))),
  travel_layers = nlyr(travel_grid),
  grid_residents = round(global(pop, "sum", na.rm = TRUE)[[1]]),
  ons_residents = sum(areas$pop)
)
```

```{r grid-numbers, include = FALSE}
grid_total <- global(pop, "sum", na.rm = TRUE)[[1]]
grid_gap <- round(100 * (1 - grid_total / sum(areas$pop)))
cell_residents <- values(pop, mat = FALSE)
under_50 <- round(100 * mean(cell_residents[!is.na(cell_residents)] < 50))
```

The grid holds about `r grid_gap`% fewer residents than the ONS mid-2024
estimate in `cornwall_lsoa`. The two are different sources and dates: choose
one for an analysis and say which. In the travel layers, `NA` marks cells with
no residents, pairs with no road connection and journeys over 180 minutes. The
map shows residents per cell in six classes.

```{r pop-map, fig.alt = "Raster map of the WorldPop 2020 population grid for Cornwall and the Isles of Scilly in residents per cell, in six classes; most cells hold fewer than 50 residents and the towns stand out with several hundred or more."}
# The outline of Cornwall and the Isles of Scilly, in the grid's coordinates
outline <- cornwall_lsoa |>
  st_union() |>
  st_transform(crs(pop)) |>
  vect()

plot(
  pop,
  breaks = c(0, 10, 50, 100, 500, 1000, 5000),
  col = hcl.colors(6, "YlGnBu", rev = TRUE),
  axes = FALSE,
  main = "WorldPop 2020: residents per cell (about 1 km)",
  plg = list(title = "Residents")
)
lines(outline, lwd = 0.6)
```

Of the populated cells, `r under_50`% hold fewer than 50 residents, and the
towns stand out with several hundred or more. The FCA guides use the grid, and
the allocation guides use the registered residents of the small areas.

## The Isles of Scilly and the mainland

The Isles of Scilly have one small area and one practice, St Mary's Health
Centre (`L82017`). Road travel times cannot cross the sea, so every travel
time between the islands and the mainland is `NA`. The code counts the unknown
times in the small-area matrix.

```{r scilly}
c(
  unknown = sum(is.na(cornwall_travel)),
  scilly_area = sum(is.na(cornwall_travel[areas$scilly, ])),
  scilly_practice = sum(is.na(cornwall_travel[, gp$scilly]))
)
```

The unknown times are the Scilly area's row (to the `r sum(!gp$scilly)`
mainland practices) and the Scilly practice's column (from the
`r sum(!areas$scilly)` mainland areas). The islands do have access to the
mainland, by boat and air, which these travel times do not represent. Rather
than treat the islands as cut off, the guides model **mainland Cornwall
only**: `r sum(!areas$scilly)` small areas and `r sum(!gp$scilly)` practices,
selected with the `scilly` column. Mainland residents registered with the
Scilly practice or outside Cornwall then count as registered outside mainland
Cornwall. [Bringing your own data](data-prep.html) shows what the unknown
times do to an FCA index when the islands are kept.

## The inputs used in the guides

The guides start from one of two short recipes, so that all of them model the
same mainland. Both prepare the data with `prep_data()`, which lines the
inputs up by ID for `spax()`, the function that runs a model on them.

### A grid, for the FCA indices

An FCA index measures supply per resident, counting nearby practices more than
distant ones. The FCA guides compute it on
the population grid and the travel stack. The recipe keeps the mainland
practices, then only the cells with a travel time to every one of them, so
that no populated cell has an unknown travel time.

```{r recipe-grid}
gp <- cornwall_gp |>
  filter(!scilly) |>
  st_drop_geometry()
pop <- read_spax_example("cornwall_pop.tif")
travel_grid <- read_spax_example("cornwall_gp_travel.tif")[[gp$practice]]
# Keep cells with a travel time to every mainland practice
pop <- trim(mask(pop, sum(travel_grid)))
travel_grid <- crop(travel_grid, pop)
grid_data <- prep_data(pop, gp, travel_grid, id_col = "practice", supply_cols = "gp_fte_extg")
grid_data
```

`[[gp$practice]]` picks the travel layers of the mainland practices by name,
in the table's order. `sum(travel_grid)` is `NA` wherever any layer is `NA`,
so the mask keeps exactly the cells with complete travel. `trim()` drops the
empty margin the islands leave behind, and `crop()` cuts the travel stack to
the trimmed grid.

The mainland grid holds
`r format(round(global(pop, "sum", na.rm = TRUE)[[1]]), big.mark = ",")`
residents, against `r format(round(grid_total), big.mark = ",")` in the full
grid. As the print says, `grid_data` points to the rasters rather than copying
them: run the recipe again in a new session instead of saving it.

### Small areas, for the allocation model

The allocation model gives each small area's residents a probability of
registering at each practice, or with the outside option: a practice outside
the data. It runs on numeric inputs named by ID: demand (the people of each
small area who may register), supply by practice and the travel matrix
between them. Demand is the registered residents of each area, so it counts
the same people as the registrations. The mainland rows and columns of
`cornwall_travel` have no unknown times. The labels in `metadata` record units
and dates with the data. spax keeps them with every result and does not
convert them.

```{r recipe-areas}
areas <- cornwall_lsoa |>
  filter(!scilly) |>
  st_drop_geometry()
gp <- cornwall_gp |>
  filter(!scilly) |>
  st_drop_geometry()
travel <- cornwall_travel[areas$lsoa, gp$practice]
demand <- setNames(areas$registered, areas$lsoa)
supply <- setNames(gp$gp_fte_extg, gp$practice)
d <- prep_data(demand, supply, travel, metadata = list(
  demand_units = "registered residents", demand_period = "July 2026",
  supply_units = "GP FTE excluding GPs in training", supply_period = "June 2026",
  travel_units = "minutes"))
flows <- obs_flows(cornwall_flows, origin = "lsoa", facility = "practice", count = "patients")
d
flows
```

```{r outside-gap, include = FALSE}
at_mainland <- cornwall_flows$lsoa %in% areas$lsoa &
  cornwall_flows$practice %in% gp$practice
outside_gap <- sum(areas$registered) - sum(cornwall_flows$patients[at_mainland])
```

`d` holds `r nrow(areas)` small areas (origins) by `r nrow(gp)` practices
(facilities), all active, that is, with demand above zero. Their demand is
larger than their registrations at mainland practices by
`r format(outside_gap, big.mark = ",")` residents: those registered elsewhere,
whom the outside option stands for. `flows` names its loss, Poisson, which is
how a fit compares modeled with observed counts.

`obs_flows()` declares the observed registrations from the long table, which
still includes the Isles of Scilly. When `spax()` fits a model, it matches the
counts to the data and says in a message which counts it sets aside.
[Bringing your own data](data-prep.html#observed-counts-in-a-long-table)
explains that message.

## Sources, dates and licenses

| Data | Objects | Source and date | License |
|:--|:--|:--|:--|
| Registrations | `cornwall_gp`, `cornwall_lsoa`, `cornwall_flows` | NHS England, Patients Registered at a GP Practice, July 2026 | Open Government Licence v3.0 |
| GP workforce | `cornwall_gp` | NHS England, General Practice Workforce, 30 June 2026 | Open Government Licence v3.0 |
| Practice locations | `cornwall_gp` | ONS Postcode Directory, November 2025 | Open Government Licence v3.0; contains OS and Royal Mail data |
| Boundaries, centroids, population | `cornwall_lsoa` | ONS LSOA 2021 boundaries and rural-urban classification, population-weighted centroids, mid-2024 population estimates | Open Government Licence v3.0; contains OS data |
| Population grid | `cornwall_pop.tif` | WorldPop, 2020 UN-adjusted 1 km estimates | Creative Commons Attribution 4.0 |
| Travel times | `cornwall_travel`, `cornwall_gp_travel.tif` | Derived by the package author from the Malaria Atlas Project 2019 motorized friction surface (Weiss et al. 2020) | Creative Commons Attribution; version not yet confirmed |

Each source keeps the license given in the table. The package's MIT license
covers its code only. The registrations and the workforce are from 2026, the
population grid from 2020, the small-area
population from mid-2024 and the road network from about 2019, so keep the
dates in mind when reading results. The full attributions, with the required
wording for each source, are installed with the package:

```{r copyrights, eval = FALSE}
file.show(system.file("COPYRIGHTS", package = "spax"))
```
